book:666634.description: Great modern American supernaturalist brilliantly surveys history of genre to 1930s, summarizing, evaluating scores of books, including works by Poe, Bierce, M.R. James, "Monk" Lewis, many others. Praised by critics as diverse as Edmund Wilson and Vincent Starrett.

book:web_cb4d3050.description: An unfinished Gothic fragment published in 1773 by Anna Laetitia Barbauld (then known as Miss Aikin), included in her collection 'Lessons for Children' and later recognized as an early example of Gothic horror literature. It was praised for its effective evocation of terror.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft references Mrs. Barbauld's fragment 'Sir Bertrand' as an early and skillful Gothic imitation of Walpole, noting its effective use of supernatural dread.
H.P. Lovecraft notes this juvenile work as an example of James’s ability to infuse even lighter fiction with subtle supernatural undertones, demonstrating the pervasiveness of his thematic concerns.

book:5130635.description:
The follow-up volume to "Ghost Stories of an Antiquary" collects seven more of Montague Rhodes James's classic horror stories, including "A School Story," "The Rose Garden," "Casting the Runes," and "Martin's Close."
"...gifted with an almost diabolic power of calling horror by gentle steps from the midst of prosaic daily life, is the scholarly Montague Rhodes James, Provost of Eton College, antiquary of note, and recognized authority on mediaeval manuscripts and cathedral history. Dr. James, long fond of t...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft references this second collection to illustrate the evolution and consistency of James’s method in crafting subtle, antiquarian-based terror.

book:15720488.description: The story of Paxton, an antiquarian and archaeologist who holidays in "Seaburgh" and inadvertently stumbles across one of the lost crowns of Anglia, which legendarily protect the country from invasion.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft references this collection as a culmination of James’s technique, where historical detail and quiet dread combine to produce enduring horror.

book:web_6828dac4.description: A posthumously published novella by Nathaniel Hawthorne, first appearing in 1883 in the collection 'Dr. Grimshawe's Secret and Other Tales'. The story is set in Salem, Massachusetts, and features a mysterious house adjoining the Charter Street Burying Ground, blending psychological horror with Gothic elements.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this novel as an example of Hawthorne’s subtle infusion of supernatural unease into otherwise mundane settings, particularly tied to Salem’s historical atmosphere.

book:12399131.description: In a sleepy little New England village stands a dark, weather-beaten, many-gabled house. This brooding mansion is haunted by a centuries-old curse that casts the shadow of ancestral sin upon the last four members of the distinctive Pyncheon family of Salem. The greed and haughty pride of the Pyncheon family through the generations is mirrored in the gloomy decay of their seven-gabled mansion, where the family's enfeebled and impoverished relations now live. Mysterious deaths threaten the living. Musty docum...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft identifies this novel as Hawthorne’s supreme contribution to American weird literature, praising its atmospheric mastery and thematic depth rooted in ancestral guilt.
H.P. Lovecraft references Hawthorne's collection of myth retellings as a vehicle for his gentle, whimsical expression of the weird, distinct from his darker works.

book:web_21846bfb.description: A collection of extraordinary and supernatural tales compiled by Phlegon of Tralles, a Greek freedman and librarian under Emperor Hadrian. The work includes accounts of ghosts, prophecies, and miraculous events, and was widely referenced in antiquity and later in literary studies of the supernatural.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft identifies Phlegon's compilation as an early source of weird tales, specifically mentioning the corpse-bride story of 'Philinnion and Machates'.

book:web_b168a978.description: A prose novel by Irish poet Thomas Moore, published in 1827, expanding on his earlier poem 'Alciphron' and exploring themes of hedonism, philosophy, and the macabre in a Gothic context.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft notes Moore's expansion of a poem into a novel, crediting The Epicurean with infusing genuine horror into its subterranean supernatural scenes.

book:8735156.description: Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer-Lytton (1803-1873) was an English novelist, poet, playwright, and politician. He was a florid, popular writer of his day, who coined such phrases as "the great unwashed," and "the pen is mightier than the sword."
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites A Strange Story as a superior work in Bulwer-Lytton’s oeuvre, highlighting its powerful incantation scenes and evocation of cosmic horror.

book:11066662.description: MARY E. WILKINS FREEMAN (1852-1930) was best known in her own day as a regional writer, for her stories depicting the bleak life of the New England rural populace of her day. Her best collections in his mode are A HUMBLE ROMANCE AND OTHER STORIES (1887) and A NEW ENGLAND NUN AND OTHER STORIES (1891). She is probably better remembered today for her ghost stories, first collected in THE WIND IN THE ROSE-BUSH AND OTHER STORIES OF THE SUPERNATURAL (1903), which likewise makes use of deftly-observed regional det...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this collection as a source of powerful, atmospherically grounded American horror stories.
H.P. Lovecraft cites these specific tales by White as exemplars of his dream-inspired, uniquely convincing brand of weird fiction.

book:6234638.description: Dive into this classic from the singular mind of Edgar Allan Poe, who is widely regarded as the master of short horror fiction. "The Fall of the House of Usher" recounts the terrible events that befall the last remaining members of the once-illustrious Usher clan before it is -- quite literally -- rent asunder. With amazing economy, Poe plunges the reader into a state of deliciously agonizing suspense. It's a must-read for fans of the golden era of horror writing.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft references Poe's story as a benchmark for comparing the atmospheric horror in Shiel's "The House of Sounds".

book:6917222.description: First published in 1892, "The Yellow Wallpaper" is written as the secret journal of a woman who, failing to relish the joys of marriage and motherhood, is sentenced to a country rest cure. Though she longs to write, her husband and doctor forbid it, prescribing instead complete passivity. In the involuntary confinement of her bedroom, the hero creates a reality of her own beyond the hypnotic pattern of the faded yellow wallpaper--a pattern that has come to symbolize her own imprisonment. Narrated with super...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft elevates this story to classic status for its psychological depth and its masterful depiction of creeping madness.

book:25150823.description: The King in Yellow - recently featured in HBO's hit series True Detective - is a classic collection of 10 short stories, the reading of which will curse one to a terrible fate. You have been warned! This edition features an introduction by H.P. Lovecraft. As an added bonus, it includes "An Inhabitant of Carcosa," by Ambrose Bierce, another related story. H.P. Lovecraft wrote: "The King in Yellow, a series of vaguely connected short stories...whose perusal brings fright, madness, and spectral tragedy, really...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this work as a landmark in cosmic horror, noting its central fictional book as a catalyst for madness and its influence on later weird fiction.
H.P. Lovecraft lists Brood of the Witch-Queen as a significant work in the post-Dracula wave of supernatural horror fiction.
H.P. Lovecraft cites this work as a prime example of the conte cruel, highlighting its extreme emotional torment and its status as a pinnacle of macabre short fiction.

book:10757634.description:
A book that deeply influenced the young Freud & was the inspiration for many artists, The Temptation of Saint Anthonywas Flaubert's lifelong work, 30 years in the making. Based on the story of the 3rd-century saint who lived on an isolated mountaintop in the Egyptian desert, it's a fantastical rendering of one night during which Anthony is besieged by carnal temptations & philosophical doubt.
This edition features the distinguished Lafcadio Hearn translation, which translator Richard Sieburth calls a splend...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites Flaubert's work as a classic example of fevered, imagery-rich prose translated by Hearn.

book:19278544.description: Lilith, written by the father of fantasy literature, George MacDonald, was first published in 1895. Its importance was recognized in its later revival in paperback by Ballantine Books as the fifth volume of the celebrated Ballantine Adult Fantasy series in September, 1969. Lilith is considered among the darkest of MacDonald's works, and among the most profound. It is a story concerning the nature of life, death and salvation. Many believe MacDonald is arguing for Christian universalism, or the idea that all...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft identifies Lilith as a uniquely bizarre and compelling work of supernatural fiction, favoring its earlier version.

book:17669440.description: Ambrose Bierce is one of the most notable and influential American horror authors, bridging the period between Poe and Lovecraft. His spare precise prose and sardonic wit easily set him apart from a genre full of melodrama and purple prose. This is the second collection of his short stories published during his lifetime, and contains such classics of American horror as 'Haita the Shepherd', 'An Inhabitant of Carcosa', 'The Death of Halpin Frayser', and 'The Damned Thing'.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this book as one of the two primary collections containing Bierce’s weird tales, establishing its canonical status in American weird literature.
H.P. Lovecraft cites this book as one of the two primary collections containing Bierce’s weird tales, establishing its canonical status in American weird literature.

book:27869748.description:
THE TURN OF THE SCREW, originally published in 1898, is a gothic ghost story novella written by Henry James.
Due to its original content, the novella became a favorite text of academics who subscribe to New Criticism. The novella has had differing interpretations, often mutually exclusive. Many critics have tried to determine the exact nature of the evil hinted at by the story. However, others have argued that the true brilliance of the novella comes with its ability to create an intimate confusion and susp...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft acknowledges James's stylistic flaws but praises this work as a masterful example of psychological and supernatural horror.
H.P. Lovecraft cites this novel as an example of restrained American horror, noting its effective use of supernatural suggestion and atmospheric detail.

book:web_e980171a.description: A collection of fantasy short stories by Lord Dunsany, first published in 1910, featuring mythic and otherworldly tales set in imaginary lands. The title story involves a city at the edge of a jungle and divine laughter that heralds doom.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this play as an example of Dunsany’s use of auditory dread and fatalistic myth, linking it to literary tradition while maintaining his unique cosmic tone.

book:365882.description:
Set against the religious struggles and civil wars of seventeenth century Scotland, John Buchan's Witch Woodis a gripping atmospheric tale in the spirit of Stevenson and Neil Munro.
As a moderate presbyterian minister, young David Sempill disputes with the extremists of his faith, as all around, the defeated remnants of Montrose's men are being harried and slaughtered.
There are still older conflicts to be faced however, symbolised by the presence of the Melanudrigall Wood, a last remnant of the ancient Cal...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft commends Witch Wood for its vivid depiction of occult survivals in Scottish folklore, despite its slow pacing.

book:1221719.description: Written in his distinctively dazzling manner, Oscar Wilde's story of a fashionable young man who sells his soul for eternal youth and beauty is the author's most popular work. The tale of Dorian Gray's moral disintegration caused a scandal when it first appeared in 1890, but though Wilde was attacked for the novel's corrupting influence, he responded that there is, in fact, "a terrible moral in Dorian Gray." Just a few years later, the book and the aesthetic/moral dilemma it presented became issues in the t...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft highlights Wilde's novel as a core work of weird literature for its supernatural portrait motif and moral decay theme.

book:27873069.description: A man's neighbour in an apartment appears to be dabbling in the black arts. Another story inspired by Blackwood's time in New York. The events depicted are likely based on Blackwood's learning whilst a member of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft references this tale as an example of Blackwood’s ability to evoke terrifying presences summoned from beyond, using psychological and spatial horror.

book:13298131.description:
The Book of Wonder is the seventh book and fifth original short story collection of Irish fantasy writer Lord Dunsany, considered a major influence on the work of J. R. R. Tolkien, H. P. Lovecraft, Ursula LeGuin and others. It was first published in hardcover by William Heinemann in November, 1912, and has been reprinted a number of times since. A 1918 edition from the Modern Library was actually a combined edition with Time and the Gods.
The book collects fourteen fantasy short stories by the author.
Sourc...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this collection as a key example of Dunsany’s mythopoeic horror, highlighting its eerie, fairy-tale-like entities that evoke cosmic dread through subtle suggestion.

book:1294145.description: A sharply written tale of adventure on the seas, The Phantom Shipwill grip the reader from the outset, drawing one into the vibrant world of Captain Marryat's imagination. It is the story of one Phillip Vanderdecken, and his search for a piece of the "one true cross." From the writer who inspired Herman Melville to take to the seas, this is an exciting work which combines the thrill of the narrative chase with an examination of the theme of religious tolerance, which has possibly a greater resonance today.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites The Phantom Ship as a significant supernatural work based on the Flying Dutchman legend, praising its memorability.

book:18338834.description: This classic novel of the weird supernatural, first published in 1908, was an important influence on H. P. Lovecraft. In the ruins of an ancient stone house in Ireland is found the diary of an elderly man who lived alone with his sister and their pets, and who longed for his lost love. The diary tells of how the man explores a cyclopean cavern beneath the house and fights off swarms of white pig-like monsters pouring up from below. Then, in a visionary sequence, he breaks through to an alternate space-time....
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft elevates this book as the pinnacle of Hodgson’s output, highlighting its unique depiction of cosmic horror and the narrator’s journey through eternity.
H.P. Lovecraft cites this book as a foundational work of cosmic horror, praising its brooding menace and nautical erudition despite its romantic letdown.

book:6519002.description:
Originally written in 1896.
This book was converted from its physical edition to the digital format by a community of volunteers. You may find it for free on the web. Purchase of the Kindle edition includes wireless delivery.
A strange, fearless woman. Wolves prowling the night. Mysteries. The world outside the cozy house can be dangerous. Being prepared does not always mean you will survive.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft notes Housman's novelette as a powerful, folklore-infused treatment of werewolf mythology.

book:web_8dbdf714.description: A short story by Arthur Machen, first published in 1915, blending mystical themes with the horror genre; it explores the return of ancient spiritual forces, tied to the Holy Grail legend and the context of World War I.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites this work as a transcendent example of mysticism emerging from horror, linking it to the Graal legend and the wartime context.

book:6298312.description: In ill health following a stroke, Sir Walter Scott wrote 'Letters on Demonology and Witchcraft' at the behest of his son-in-law, J. G. Lockhart, who worked for a publishing firm. The book proved popular and Scott was paid six hundred pounds, which he desperately needed. (Despite his success as a novelist, Scott was almost ruined when the Ballantyne publishing firm, where he was a partner, went bankrupt in 1826.) 'Letters' was written when educated society believed itself in enlightened times due to advances...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites Scott's nonfiction work as a authoritative compilation of European witch-lore, highlighting its enduring scholarly value.
H.P. Lovecraft cites Frankenstein as a horror-classic of all time, praising its enduring impact and noting its origin in a literary competition.

book:web_9e06b8d8.description: A Gothic horror novella published in 1819, widely regarded as the first modern vampire story in English literature. It was initially attributed to Lord Byron but later confirmed as the work of John William Polidori, who was Byron's physician and companion during the famous 1816 Geneva gathering that also inspired Mary Shelley's Frankenstein.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft acknowledges Polidori's story as a successful development of a competing horror narrative from the same literary gathering.

book:web_342aa333.description: A Gothic novel published in 1764, widely regarded as the first Gothic fiction work, featuring supernatural elements, medieval settings, and dramatic suspense that influenced the horror genre.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft credits Walpole as the founder of the Gothic horror novel, citing 'The Castle of Otranto' as the seminal work that established the genre's formula despite its artistic flaws.

book:web_57bdf8db.description: A psychological horror novel by American author Leonard Cline, published posthumously in 1927. It explores themes of identity, madness, and the supernatural through the story of a man who discovers a hidden chamber in his house that allows him to relive and alter his past.
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft praises this novel as a profound exploration of hereditary memory and the dangers of defying natural limits through obsessive recall.
